text.en: Can an elephant and a stray dog be best friends? They are so different in size, in food and in the way they live. Yet this story from the Jataka tradition says real friendship does not depend on being alike. Let us meet Gajaraj and Buntee.

Friends are important because we play, share and feel happy with them. The book asks you to complete sentences like: with my friend I play, with my friend I feel happy. The title uses the word unlikely, which means not expected to happen. An unlikely friendship is one between two people or animals you would not expect to be friends.
Gajaraj is an elephant who lives in the best booth of the royal stables. The king is fond of him and orders that he be well looked after. Despite all the royal comforts, Gajaraj is sad because he has no friends. The only one he talks to is the mahout, or elephant trainer. The mahout is kind, serves food and gives Gajaraj a bath in the elephant pond every day. He is a good caretaker, but he is not a friend. Gajaraj thinks that he wishes to have a friend to play with.
One evening a stray dog wanders into the stable, tired and hungry. Gajaraj pushes some of his own food towards the dog. The dog wags his tail to say thanks, eats and falls asleep. The next morning the mahout finds the dog, does not mind and throws him some crumbs. He notices that Gajaraj likes the company. At bath time the dog follows the elephant. Gajaraj sprays water playfully, the dog yelps because he hates showers, and the mahout laughs. On the way home Gajaraj lifts the dog on to his back and the dog enjoys the ride.
A farmer passing by sees the dog and shouts Buntee. The dog runs to him and the farmer hugs him, because he had been searching for his lost dog. The mahout has no objection to the farmer taking the dog home. The farmer puts a rope around the dog and says, come Buntee, let us go home. When the rope is pulled, Buntee realises he is being taken away from his friend. He yelps and the elephant winces, but neither the farmer nor the mahout notices that both friends have tears.
Gajaraj refuses his favourite food at lunch, and again that night and the next day. The mahout thinks it may be indigestion, but checks his tummy and finds nothing wrong. Then he guesses that Gajaraj is missing his friend, the dog. At the farmer's house Buntee also refuses food. The farmer remembers Buntee's happy face on the elephant's back and understands he is missing his friend. He says he cannot see the dog go hungry, removes the rope and tells him to go to his friend.
Though weak, the dog springs up, licks the farmer's hand once and runs all the way to the stable. Gajaraj picks him up with his trunk and swings him joyfully. The mahout is relieved and quickly brings food, saying both should eat first. The farmer, who followed the dog, joins them. Watching the two friends eat, the mahout hugs the farmer and says it is not only Gajaraj who has found a friend, since he has found one too. So in the end the unlikely friendship also makes new friends of the mahout and the farmer. The lesson is that friendship is about caring and not about being alike, and that a good person lets a friend go to a friend.
Opposites can be formed by adding letters before a word: un- makes unhappy, in- makes incorrect, dis- makes disconnect and mis- makes misuse. From the story: kind and unkind, touched and untouched, appeared and disappeared, sad and joyous or happy. Other opposites in the puzzle are yelped and whispered, awake and asleep, relieved and worried, and started and finished.
Simple past tense shows an action that was completed in the past, such as looked, gave, noticed, went, told, asked, felt. Past progressive tense shows an action that was going on at a past time. It uses was or were plus verb with ing, such as was munching, was looking, was missing. Past perfect tense shows an action that was completed before another past action. It uses had plus the third form of the verb, such as had ordered, had followed, had tied, had remained. For example, the farmer noticed that Buntee was sad. He had tied Buntee with a rope the day before.
Neither and nor connect two negative choices. For example, neither the farmer nor the mahout noticed the tears. Either and or give a choice between two things you want. For example, Rohit wants to play either cricket or kho-kho. Practice: neither Shikha nor Anuj likes to tell stories; either Bhavesh or Abha made this painting. In the speaking task, talk with your friend about what you both like and how you are different, using words like both, but, and, like, unlike, neither, nor, either and or.

problem.en: Choose the right form: The farmer came back and ____ (noticed / was noticing / had noticed) that Buntee was sad. He ____ (tied / was tying / had tied) Buntee with a rope the day before.

text.en: First, check the order of events: tying came before noticing.

why.en: The earlier past action takes the past perfect.

text.en: The first blank is the main action, noticed. The second blank is the earlier action, had tied.

why.en: Had tied shows tying was finished before the farmer noticed.

problem.en: Fill in with neither/nor or either/or: ____ Shikha ____ Anuj likes to tell stories.

text.en: The sentence is negative about both people, so we use the negative pair.

why.en: Neither and nor go together to join two negative choices.

text.en: Write: Neither Shikha nor Anuj likes to tell stories.

why.en: The verb likes is singular because Anuj is singular.

prompt.en: Tell how Gajaraj and Buntee proved that friendship is more than being alike.

requiredIdeas.en: An elephant and a dog are very different.
Gajaraj shared food with the dog and they played together.
The farmer let the dog go because he understood their bond.

commonMisconceptions.en: Gajaraj was fed by the dog.
The farmer kept Buntee tied because he was a bad person.

points.en: The Unlikely Best Friends is a story about an elephant, Gajaraj, and a dog, Buntee.
Both friends refused food when they were separated, and the farmer set Buntee free.
The mahout and farmer also found a friend.
Prefixes un-, in-, dis- and mis- make opposites.
Simple past, past progressive and past perfect show different kinds of past actions; neither-nor joins two negatives.
